claims.quote: Applications for aged care have for the last year been determined using AI, not human beings. The Albanese government implemented a system last year which featured strict prohibition of human override. Expert, qualified human-needs assessors were explicitly barred from altering or overriding the algorithm's outputs, even when they knew a decision was clinically wrong.
claims.claim: Since late 2025 Australian aged-care (Support at Home) classifications have been set by an AI tool that assessors are barred from overriding.
claims.source_name: FOI documents reveal how human override disappeared from Support at Home assessments
claims.source_notes: Reporting confirms that from 1 Nov 2025 assessors had no discretion to override ongoing Support at Home classifications. Assessor concerns were raised within weeks of launch, so the public date is set to 2025-11 (approximate).
claims.incident_accuracy_note: Reporting describes the Integrated Assessment Tool as a rules/algorithm-based tool and not as AI, and departmental guidance said it was not an automated process; the speaker calls it AI with no human involvement.
claims.vintage_rationale: Incident; the removal of human override is the evidence.

claims.quote: Critics noted that the rigid computer program frequently failed to capture the complex realities of ageing

claims.vintage_rationale: Consistent with assessor, doctor and later Ombudsman criticism of the tool through 2026.

claims.incident_accuracy_note: Search found reports that review requests more than doubled (to 834, later 2,208), not a sixfold rise; the sixfold figure is unverified.
claims.vintage_rationale: Incident claim; public date of the review figures not established.

coder_notes: The speaker calls the Support at Home Integrated Assessment Tool "AI", so under the v0.2 rule the claims are included. Reporting calls it an algorithm. The sixfold appeals figure could not be verified, and its event dates are left null.

claims.vintage_rationale: Incident; public disclosure on 24 Sep 2026 is the evidence date.

coder_notes: The agent is not named in the speech (an OpenAI agent per reporting). The technique is disputed in some reporting (a guest endpoint), but "breaching" matches the PM's account.

claims.quote: American courts have ruled on training for generative AI and so far have found it to be a fair use.
claims.claim: US courts that have ruled on generative AI training have so far found it to be fair use.
claims.source_name: Bartz v. Anthropic fair use ruling (N.D. Cal.)
claims.source_org: US District Court, Northern District of California
claims.source_notes: Bartz v Anthropic (23 Jun 2025) and Kadrey v Meta (25 Jun 2025) found training to be fair use, but Bartz excluded pirated library copies and Kadrey was limited to its plaintiffs. Thomson Reuters v Ross (D. Del. Feb 2025; reportedly 3d Cir. Sep 2026) rejected fair use for non-generative AI.

other_sources.name: Kadrey v. Meta fair use ruling

claims.vintage_rationale: Two 2025 district rulings found generative AI training fair use, but with significant limits (pirated copies, narrow scope), and no appellate ruling on generative AI has been found; the "so far" framing overstates settled law.

claims.quote: Generative AI doesn't substitute or compete with the products that it learns from.
claims.claim: Generative AI outputs do not substitute for or compete with the works they are trained on.
claims.vintage_rationale: Disputed: the Kadrey v Meta judge and the US Copyright Office (May 2025 pre-publication report) discussed market dilution and substitution by generative outputs (coder recall).
